issues.author: RohithKuditipudi
issues.body:
A caller that runs `execute()` on a worker thread has no way, from any other thread, to make it stop early — whether the pipeline's results are no longer needed or the process is shutting down. If the worker job that `execute()` launches never schedules (no accelerator capacity), the call blocks for 12 hours and nothing can release it sooner.

What `execute()` launches: on a fresh context it calls `_start_pool()`, which submits a coordinator job (`execution.py:502`), tells it to spawn a worker job, and waits for the first worker to register — up to `ZEPHYR_WORKERS_READY_WAIT`, default 12 h (`execution.py:532-533`). The handles to these jobs are held in variables local to the call (`execution.py:646`); nothing is assigned to the context object, and `self._state` stays `NEW`.

What `shutdown()` does: it stops what the context has registered — the pool that only `start()` assigns (`execution.py:550`) — and returns immediately for state `NEW` (`execution.py:689`). During `execute()` it therefore has no effect: the jobs it would need to stop are reachable only from inside the blocked call. Calling `start()` first does not help: `start()` holds `_state_lock` across the same first-worker wait (`execution.py:550`), and `shutdown()` blocks acquiring that lock (`execution.py:684`).

What changed: before #7145, `execute()` stored its coordinator job on the instance (`self._coordinator_job`) and `shutdown()` terminated that job — workers included, via cascading termination — from any thread at any point in the call. #7145 moved the pool into the `execute()` call and rewrote `shutdown()` around the `NEW`/`OWNER` state machine; cancelling a running `execute()` was dropped with no replacement.

Observed in production, 2026-08-22/23: a driver needed to cancel `execute()` calls whose work other pools had already completed. The v5litepod worker jobs never scheduled (`Insufficient TPUs (need 4, available 0)`); `shutdown()` at ~02:00 UTC had no effect, and each blocked call held its thread until the 12 h wait expired at ~11:20 UTC. The only unstick was killing the coordinator jobs out-of-band.

Done when: `shutdown()` (or an equivalent) promptly cancels a running `execute()`, including one still waiting for its first worker. One shape: register the coordinator group on the context at creation, before the blocking waits; deregister when the pool ends; have `shutdown()` stop registered live groups regardless of state.

## Summary

This eval experiment tried to reproduce Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index Terminal-Bench 2.1 scores on Marin for four large MoE baselines using Terminus 2, three attempts per task, a 250-turn limit, a 7,200-second agent timeout, and the pinned TB2.1 dataset. The main result is mixed. Nemotron 3 Ultra 550B A55B NVFP4 reproduced the AAII point estimate almost exactly at 54.09% versus 53.93%. Qwen3.5-122B-A10B-FP8 was still preliminary in the posted table, at 42.34% versus 47.57% with 110/111 completed trials and 156 trials remaining. DeepSeek-V4-Flash-0731 cleared the infrastructure-success gate but missed parity badly, scoring 56.23% versus AAII's 78.65% with no confirmed protocol discrepancy. GLM-5.2 AWQ INT4 produced no valid cohort because the checkpoint could not be served with the required context under the tested single-node geometry. The follow-up work is to finish Qwen, isolate the DeepSeek score gap, and rerun GLM with a serving geometry that preserves the intended context budget.

WHAT THIS IS: The purpose of this experiment was to try to reproduce AAII tb2.1 eval scores on the Marin cluster on some strong baselines.

RESULT: Picked four models; Qwen3.5-122B-A10B-FP8, DeepSeek-V4-Flash-0731, Nemotron 3 Ultra 550B A55B NVFP4, GLM-5.2 AWQ INT4. 🤖 ## Experiment summary

This experiment compares Marin's Terminal-Bench 2.1 results with the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index (AAII) for four large MoE models. The protocol uses Terminus 2, three attempts per task (267 trials), a 250-turn limit, a 7,200-second agent timeout, and the pinned `terminal-bench/terminal-bench-2-1@sha256:7d7bdc1cbedad549fc1140404bd4dc45e5fd0ea7c4186773687d177ad3a0699a` dataset. Marin used Daytona sandboxes; AAII used E2B.

| Model | AAII | Marin | Delta | Scoreable trials | Infrastructure success | Status |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---|
| Nemotron 3 Ultra 550B A55B NVFP4 | 53.93% | 54.09% | +0.16 pp | 257/267 | 96.25% | Reproduced |
| Qwen3.5-122B-A10B-FP8 | 47.57% | 42.34% | -5.23 pp | 110/111 completed | 99.10% | Preliminary; 156 trials remain |
| DeepSeek-V4-Flash-0731 | 78.65% | 56.23% | -22.42 pp | 265/267 | 99.25% | Valid Marin result; parity failed |
| GLM-5.2 AWQ INT4 | 77.90% | — | — | 0/267 | 0.00% | No valid cohort |

The Qwen rerun aligns the 262,144-token serving context and 81,920-token generation limit across vLLM and Terminus 2. Its current 42.34% mean comprises 48 successes and 62 zeros. Thirteen `AgentTimeoutError` trials received verifier scores and are valid; one `VerifierTimeoutError` is an infrastructure failure.

Nemotron reproduces the AAII point estimate within 0.16 percentage points. DeepSeek clears the 90% infrastructure gate but remains 22.42 points below AAII with no confirmed protocol discrepancy. GLM did not produce a valid result because the AWQ checkpoint could not be served with the required context under the tested single-node geometry; pipeline parallelism or B200 capacity remains to be tested.

Checkpoint and environment differences limit the comparison. AAII evaluated unquantized Qwen and GLM checkpoints and BF16 Nemotron, while Marin used Qwen FP8, GLM AWQ INT4, and Nemotron NVFP4. DeepSeek used the same checkpoint family. The sandbox provider also differs.

Next steps are to finish the Qwen cohort, isolate the DeepSeek score gap, and rerun GLM with a serving geometry that preserves the intended context budget.

# Snowball 262K checkpoint guide

For Snowball, @ClassicLarry did some basic tweaking of arch. and I did some basic tweaking of data for long context. Arch. stuff is the basic lever of adding gain to the QK norm scaling to try to decrease the attention entropy issues from https://allenai.org/papers/olmpool. Data stuff is just keeping domain distribution the same, and unweighting long context documents from https://arxiv.org/abs/2409.12181

There are a total of 5 checkpoints to compare long-context training choices, with each being slightly better by basic metrics (which may or may not transfer to RL). Each ran from step 156,000 to step 157,000 at 262K context and are otherwise the same.

issues.author: penfever
issues.body:
A structured review response that is truncated on the model side ended up as a cached entry in a completion-gated query cache, and bounded retry loops replay it instead of recovering the row.

Observed in a SAMPLE review campaign (pinned V3 reviewer, cache `s3://marin-us-east-02a/marin/rl-data/atlas/sample-qc/request-cache-v3-2026.11.15.1-code`):

Reproduce:
1. Task `tasktrove-taco-8e0838d71891a2a697074e46528075b50d47f39a0cc52c2925d3f123312532aa` fails its first review attempt with detail `Incomplete or truncated structured response` (finish/length guard on the structured response).
2. The truncated response is nonetheless present as a cached entry under the request's cache key (verified by independent byte-level readback of the cache store).
3. A repair re-review of the same request re-issues the row across 4 bounded-repeat rounds; the row stays INVALID with the same detail. The row only recovers when the follow-up runs against a fresh versioned cache namespace.

Why this is a bug rather than a data problem: the only cache write path (`taskcompendium/pipeline/query_cache.py` `_store_completion`) is gated by `valid_completion` = `review_records(output, [task_id])[0].status == REVIEWED`, which should reject a truncated structured response. A truncated entry in the store therefore means either the store-time validation accepted a truncated payload (validation gap) or an ungated write path exists. Additionally, the read path (`_cached_completions`) treats an invalid cached entry as a miss but does not invalidate it, so the entry survives indefinitely and every future re-request re-parses and re-rejects it.

Expected:
- Truncated structured responses must never be cached (tighten store-time validation to the parsed typed verdict), and
- the read path should treat a cached entry whose parse fails as a miss AND invalidate/delete that entry, so bounded retries can recover the row without a fresh cache namespace.

Context: reasoning-heavy reviewers hit `finish_reason=length` frequently on long tasks (in one pass of the same campaign, 92% of responses ended `length` with 100% reasoning tokens), so truncated-structured-response entries are a common class wherever review caches are reused across passes.

comments.author: loom-oa-dev[bot]
comments.body:
🤖 ## Research

At `0169e8a4fe`, the structured parser marks `finish_reason=length` INVALID, and the cache writes only responses whose typed review status is REVIEWED. The read path applies the same validator and submits invalid entries as misses. The archived bytes establish that an invalid entry exists, but the available evidence does not yet establish that the failed retry rounds replayed it as cache hits. FineStore has no per-key invalidation operation.

Relevant code: [finish-reason guard](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/0169e8a4fe/lib/taskcompendium/src/taskcompendium/pipeline/review_requests.py#L131-L145), [typed write gate](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/0169e8a4fe/lib/taskcompendium/src/taskcompendium/pipeline/query_cache.py#L263-L269), [invalid-entry miss path](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/0169e8a4fe/lib/taskcompendium/src/taskcompendium/pipeline/query_cache.py#L168-L176), [FineStore cache API](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/0169e8a4fe/lib/finestore/src/finestore/cache.py#L97-L160).

## Proposed Fix

1. Replay the captured envelope against `review_records` at the campaign commit. For each failed round, compare `cache_hits`, `review/cache/invalid_entries`, provider batch IDs, and response bytes. This will distinguish a cache replay from a fresh response that also ended at the length limit.
2. If the write gate accepted the truncated response, fix that validator path and add a regression that checks persisted bytes. If an invalid entry is repeatedly loaded, add per-key invalidation to FineStore with explicit memory, persistent, and concurrent-writer behavior; test recovery within the same cache namespace, including prefetched reads. If retries made fresh provider calls, address the response budget or prompt path shown by those observations.
3. Run affected TaskCompendium and FineStore tests, the repository pre-commit checks and advisory review, then publish the fix through `manage-pr` with `Fixes #11509`.

issues.author: penfever
issues.body:
The trusted TaskSpec grader path runs the in-process grader command with `timeout=self.shape.verifier_timeout_sec` and raises `VerifierTimeoutError("Trusted TaskSpec grader deadline expired")` on expiry. For a set of long-conversation tasks the expiry is deterministic: every attempt of the same task exceeds the deadline, so the task records only infrastructure attempts and the source stays permanently pending — retries cannot change the outcome.

Observed in small-v16 (`2026.11.14.43/small-v16`, exited successfully); 7 sampled tasks across 4 sources, all attempts `INFRA_ERROR` with this signature:
- `Nemotron:nemotron_ultra_mopd/ultra_sft_step3200_multichallenge_len40k` (task `nemotron_ultra_mopd_ultra_sft_step3200_multichallenge_len40k-1b7017de4...`)
- `Nemotron:nemotron_ultra_rlvr1/ultra_sft_step3200_instruction_following` (task `nemotron_ultra_rlvr1_ultra_sft_step3200_instruction_following-0a7d051a...`)
- `Nemotron:nemotron_ultra_rlvr1/ultra_sft_step3200_tau_pivot`
- `Nemotron:nemotron_ultra_rlvr2/ultra_sft_step3200_instruction_following`
The affected shapes are long-context (40k-token) conversation graders, where grading time scales with conversation length.

Reproduce:
1. Run one of the listed tasks to completion (the agent turn succeeds and produces a conversation).
2. The trusted grader command is launched with the shape's `verifier_timeout_sec`; it exceeds the deadline on every attempt and `VerifierTimeoutError` is raised.
3. The attempt records `INFRA_ERROR` with no reward and the task is retried identically.

Expected: a deterministic deadline failure should be distinguishable from transient infrastructure load — e.g. a larger or conversation-length-scaled verifier budget for these shapes, or a typed "grader too slow for this shape" condition that stops retrying instead of consuming the campaign's full attempt budget.

Grader code: `vendor/harbor/src/harbor/trial/taskcompendium.py:750-752` (`result = await machine.run(Command(..., timeout=self.shape.verifier_timeout_sec))` → `raise VerifierTimeoutError("Trusted TaskSpec grader deadline expired")`).

Evidence receipts (S3, no PII): `s3://marin-rno2a/marin/rl-data/atlas/difficulty/2026.11.14.43/small-v16/trials/<sha256(source_id)>/attempts/<task_key>/*/attempt.json`.

comments.author: loom-oa-dev[bot]
comments.body:
🤖 ## Research

On draft [PR #11277](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/11277), the trusted TaskSpec grader uses the packaged verifier deadline and raises `VerifierTimeoutError` without a grade when it expires. Packaging fills missing source deadlines with a 60-second default, while declared source deadlines must match exactly. The difficulty runner spends every configured attempt on an unscored timeout, and campaign resume skips only scored tasks; neither path recognizes a repeatable grader deadline.

Relevant code:
- [`taskcompendium.py#L737-L752`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/7c86252b6c790c1d9feb1fc02ceb025359fe8303/vendor/harbor/src/harbor/trial/taskcompendium.py#L737-L752): trusted grader deadline and exception.
- [`difficulty_preparation.py#L70-L78`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/7c86252b6c790c1d9feb1fc02ceb025359fe8303/experiments/post_training/task_curation/difficulty_preparation.py#L70-L78): packaged budget.
- [`adapter.py#L105-L113`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/7c86252b6c790c1d9feb1fc02ceb025359fe8303/lib/taskcompendium/src/taskcompendium/harbor/adapter.py#L105-L113): source limit check.
- [`difficulty_trials.py#L217-L219`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/7c86252b6c790c1d9feb1fc02ceb025359fe8303/experiments/post_training/task_curation/difficulty_trials.py#L217-L219): attempt loop; [resume at L495](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/7c86252b6c790c1d9feb1fc02ceb025359fe8303/experiments/post_training/task_curation/difficulty_trials.py#L495).

## Proposed Fix

1. Inspect the seven archived task packages and attempts for their actual verifier limits and grader runtimes. Replay representative saved conversations through the trusted grader at bounded larger deadlines to measure a budget that completes; this needs no new solver turn.
2. For tasks with no declared verifier deadline, set a bounded budget during preparation based on conversation size and the measured replay, then publish new immutable task packages and a new campaign version. Preserve explicit source deadlines. Keep `small-v16` unchanged.
3. Give the trusted in-process deadline a distinct persisted exception type with its configured budget. In `difficulty_trials.py`, keep the result unscored, record a terminal pending reason for that package/budget, and stop identical attempts within a run and on resume. A new package or budget can be retried.
4. Add regressions for a long conversation that grades within the new budget, a trusted grader deadline that yields no reward, and resume behavior that avoids another identical solver attempt. Validate all seven affected tasks in the new campaign; report which grade and which remain pending with their explicit limits.

The implementation belongs in [PR #11277](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/11277) or a follow-up after it lands, since these paths are not on `main`.

issues.author: penfever
issues.body:
The TaskSpec graders shipped with reasoning-gym sources crash on free-form candidate text instead of scoring it, so the trial records an infrastructure failure and the task is left permanently pending — even though "candidate didn't produce the answer" is exactly the outcome a 0.0 reward exists for.

What breaks and impact:
- The task-shipped `/tests/grade.py` calls `scorer(candidate(Path("/app/answer.txt").read_text()), entry)`. The `reasoning_gym` scorer (`arithmetic/prime_factorization.py:55`) runs `int(factor.strip())` over the raw candidate text; when the candidate is prose (the model's chain of thought — extraction failed), `int()` raises `ValueError: invalid literal for int() with base 10: "I need to find the prime factorization of 835. ..."`.
- The grader command exits 1, `taskcompendium.runtime.grading._script_reward` maps it to `INFRA_ERROR` (`lib/taskcompendium/src/taskcompendium/runtime/grading.py:349`), and `harbor` raises `VerifierRuntimeError` (`vendor/harbor/src/harbor/trial/taskcompendium.py:559`).
- Every attempt of the affected tasks fails identically; the source's catalog row stays `pending` and the campaign's attempts are wasted.

Observed in small-v16 (`2026.11.14.43/small-v16`, exited successfully); same class in the other campaigns' pending queues:
- Sources: `TaskTrove:laion__nemotron-gym-reasoning-gym-v2`, `Nemotron:nemotron_ultra_rlvr1/ultra_sft_step3200_reasoning_gym`, `Nemotron:nemotron_ultra_rlvr2/ultra_sft_step3200_reasoning_gym`, `Reasoning Gym:reasoning_gym`.

- ~24 sampled tasks across these sources had infrastructure-only attempts with this signature (sampled up to 6 receipts per pending source).

Reproduce:
1. Run any of the reasoning-gym `prime_factorization` tasks with a candidate whose `/app/answer.txt` contains prose such as "I need to find the prime factorization of 835. Let me start by testing small prime numbers as factors: ...".
2. `_normalize_answer` raises `ValueError: invalid literal for int() with base 10: ...`; `/tests/grade.py` exits 1.

Expected: a scorer that receives a non-numeric or unparseable candidate should return reward 0.0 (a normal graded outcome), or the task should be typed `invalid_task` — never an infrastructure failure that the campaign retries identically.

issues.author: penfever
issues.body:
A second writer process opening a shared `PersistentKvCache` root while other writers are active fails its commit with a table-metadata conflict, and all entries buffered in that session are silently lost.

Observed in a large review campaign on `s3://marin-us-east-02a/marin/rl-data/atlas/full-qc/request-cache/content-v4-rubric-v2`:

Reproduce:
1. Writer A holds `PersistentKvCache.at(<root>)` (12 concurrent iris review workers with `query_cache_root=<root>`).
2. Writer B opens `PersistentKvCache.at(<root>)`, stores ~2.8k entries, closes. Commit fails:
   `FineStore cache write failed: table <BlobTables.DESCRIPTORS: 'blobs'> already exists with different metadata`
3. Re-run writer B idempotently: it re-stores the same ~2.8k entries and finds **0** of them already present, proving the first commit never landed. The loss is silent because `cache.store()` is best-effort (`taskcompendium/pipeline/query_cache.py` `_store_completion`/`_close_cache` log a warning and continue).

A related but recoverable variant on a fresh root: `Operation FineStore commit ... failed (attempt 1/100000 ...) retrying ...: conditional write failed for <root>/v2/HEAD` — this one retries and succeeds.

Expected: concurrent writers either commit through a shared-metadata protocol (merge table metadata, or per-writer descriptor shards read at lookup time) or fail with a retryable error so callers can re-flush their buffered entries. Buffered entries must not be silently dropped on a metadata conflict.

Impact: any concurrent-writer deployment (multi-worker review fleets sharing a query cache) can silently lose cached responses and redo inference.

comments.author: loom-oa-dev[bot]
comments.body:
🤖 ## Research

The reported exception comes from [table registration](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/0169e8a4feccf4db58a3b3fac50c5f24c78be473/lib/finestore/src/finestore/store.py#L233-L245): the committed `blobs` table points to a different content-addressed metadata object than this writer expects. This happens before a commit; the separate `HEAD` compare-and-swap conflict is [already retried](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/0169e8a4feccf4db58a3b3fac50c5f24c78be473/lib/finestore/src/finestore/commit.py#L310-L329). The source of the metadata difference is still unverified. The loss path is clear: the [remote cache worker](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/0169e8a4feccf4db58a3b3fac50c5f24c78be473/lib/finestore/src/finestore/cache.py#L288-L320) removes a batch before writing and only logs a failure; the [review caller](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/0169e8a4feccf4db58a3b3fac50c5f24c78be473/lib/taskcompendium/src/taskcompendium/pipeline/query_cache.py#L199-L223) also treats cache failures as warnings. No open PR for this issue or failure path was found.

## Proposed Fix

1. Read the affected root's `v2/HEAD`, its manifest, and the `blobs` metadata object. Compare the stored primary key, schema version, and conflict policy with `blob_table_metadata(BlobTables.DESCRIPTORS)` and identify the revisions used by active writers. These are small metadata reads; do not scan cache payloads.
2. If the contracts are equivalent, make registration use one canonical metadata path and cover the observed variant with a regression. If they differ, keep the mismatch explicit and migrate the cache or choose a new namespace; merging incompatible table contracts would make reads ambiguous.
3. Keep a failed remote batch available for retry and make `PersistentKvCache.close()` report uncommitted entries. Update the review caller to propagate that terminal failure so a retry can re-flush the responses. Preserve the existing bounded retry for `HEAD` conflicts.
4. Test two concurrent writers on simulated S3, a metadata mismatch after a populated batch, and successful replay after repair. Verify every key is readable from a fresh cache instance, and that a failed close never reports success.

comments.author: penfever
comments.body:
🤖 Fleet-scale confirmation from a review campaign that ran 12 concurrent workers sharing one `PersistentKvCache` root (regional S3):

**Occurrence counts per driver (primary evidence, shipped driver task logs):** every review driver logs the failure continuously. One driver's logs show **1,430 occurrences** of

```
FineStore cache write failed: table <BlobTables.DESCRIPTORS: 'blobs'> already exists with different metadata
```

over ~5 hours, still recurring (last observed at 20:42 UTC, ~every 1-2 minutes). The other drivers show the same pattern.

**Concurrency at the time:** 12 concurrent review workers on one cache root (each worker = 8 batch workers × 4 concurrent streams of long-context requests), plus one independent backfill writer — i.e. the exact multi-writer regime this issue describes.

**Impact — zero cross-run reuse during the campaign:**
- Reviews and receipts complete normally (the write path is best-effort), so the loss is invisible at the job level.
- But the commit-time cache-write guarantee is void under concurrency: the shared cache accumulated effectively nothing during the ~5h run. Any retry, resume, or future re-review of these requests replays full inference instead of reading the cache.
- Receipt-verified proof of silent loss: an idempotent backfill re-run re-stored the same ~2.8k entries with **0 present-skips**, demonstrating the earlier commit never landed.

**Two failure variants coexist:** on fresh roots, commits fail-and-retry (`Operation FineStore commit ... failed (attempt 1/100000 ...): conditional write failed for <root>/v2/HEAD`) and eventually succeed; on roots with existing table metadata and a second writer, the metadata-conflict variant above fails immediately and silently drops the buffered entries. The second variant is the one that loses data.

A serving worker can hold an H100 while tokenizer preparation remains inside `huggingface_hub.xet_get` with a zero-byte download. The observed worker made no progress for over 16 minutes after finding its model weights in the regional cache. vLLM had not started.

Reproduce the download path from Marin commit `f469c6848d805f892d69b8343402180b36f9fa89`:
1. Run this probe in a fresh worker. It uses the observed resource shape and a new per-pod tokenizer cache. The command caps the download probe at 30 minutes.

   ```bash
   uv run iris --cluster=marin job run \
     --target-cluster=cw-us-east-02a --gpu H100 --cpu 8 --memory 98GB --disk 100GB \
     --enable-extra-resources --extra cpu --priority batch --timeout 259200 \
     -e HF_HUB_DISABLE_XET 0 -e HF_HUB_CACHE /tmp/tokenizer-xet-cold -- \
     timeout 1800 python -c 'from marin.inference.model_preparation import read_tool_chat_template; read_tool_chat_template("Qwen/Qwen3-30B-A3B-Instruct-2507", revision="0d7cf23991f47feeb3a57ecb4c9cee8ea4a17bfe")'
   ```

2. If the download stalls, sample the Python stack and the cache's `.incomplete` file size/mtime twice. The serving failure was observed in `marin.inference.model_preparation.read_tool_chat_template`, which invokes this tokenizer loader before vLLM startup.
3. In the same worker, fetch `https://huggingface.co/Qwen/Qwen3-30B-A3B-Instruct-2507/resolve/0d7cf23991f47feeb3a57ecb4c9cee8ea4a17bfe/tokenizer.json` with `curl -fsSL --max-time 20` and verify the SHA below.

The stall may depend on worker/network conditions; the standalone probe has not yet been run.

Expected: tokenizer preparation completes or fails within a bounded interval, without leaving an allocated GPU waiting on an unchanged small download. Small pinned tokenizer/template assets should be ready before GPU allocation.

Evidence from 2026-11-15:

- The target `tokenizer.json` is 11,422,654 bytes, with LFS SHA256 `aeb13307a71acd8fe81861d94ad54ab689df773318809eed3cbe794b4492dae4`.
- At 23:05:07 UTC, its `.incomplete` file had 0 bytes and an age of 868.8 seconds. At 23:07:08 UTC, the same file still had 0 bytes and an age of 986.3 seconds. The other four tokenizer/config files were present.
- A 23:03:50 UTC Python stack sample showed `read_tool_chat_template → load_tokenizer → AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained → hf_hub_download → xet_get`.
- From the same worker, `curl -fsSL --max-time 20` fetched the pinned `tokenizer.json` and passed SHA256 verification.
- This occurred on attempt 2 of `new-rl-ingest-b-openresearcher-grounding-v4`. The serving job was canceled. A transport-only retry sets `HF_HUB_DISABLE_XET=1`; its result is pending.

Atlas ingest must resolve permission before conversion, census, oracle execution or QA. Missing, restricted and unrecognized terms block new ingestion and admission unless a human or coordinator records an explicit, revision-scoped exception. This issue records blocked sources and their evidence; absence of a grant is not permission.

The canonical policy reuses Marin Data Belay's Blue Oak Council v16 permissive SPDX list, CC BY/CC BY-SA and ODC-By additions, and OpenMDW pattern ([existing policy](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/experiments/data_belay/intake.py)). NC and ND terms are rejected; custom and unknown terms require review. The deterministic stage-0 checker evaluates only the pinned dataset’s own card, LICENSE files and README license statements: PASS permits ingestion, FAIL stops it, and ESCALATE goes to the user. Underlying OSS repository licenses and generated outputs alone are not ban grounds. Resolver hints do not override a permissive dataset grant; unidentified separate terms are escalated, without tracing teachers or upstream lineage.

| Source and scope | Verdict | Decision date | Status | Evidence |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Tongyi-MAI/MAI-Gym apps and task data at `dc279a3735f0d59f9b9b9806f1fc8cd99c28e6f9` | MISSING: no license grant found | 2026-11-15 | Blocked pending explicit permission | [Repository at pin](https://github.com/Tongyi-MAI/MAI-Gym/tree/dc279a3735f0d59f9b9b9806f1fc8cd99c28e6f9); [GitHub API](https://api.github.com/repos/Tongyi-MAI/MAI-Gym) reports `"license": null`; [prior investigation](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/10231#issuecomment-6231071121) |
| OpenGCUA trajectories (separate from harness code) | MISSING: no trajectory-specific grant established | 2026-11-15 | Blocked pending trajectory permission | [Trajectory publisher](https://tongyi-mai.github.io/OpenGCUA/trajectories.html); [code at pin](https://github.com/Tongyi-MAI/OpenGCUA/tree/55c33aea792b48b9c1330a514bfcc8f6d3ecc704); [prior license investigation](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/10231) |

Evidence excerpts: the MAI-Gym investigation records “its repository has no license”. OpenGCUA's trajectory publisher describes “eight frontier models”; its Apache-2.0 link points to the code repository. The prior investigation reports unlicensed trajectories, mostly closed-model outputs. That output-provenance claim is not a model-by-model permission audit. The code's Apache-2.0 grant does not establish permission for separately hosted trajectories. No text exists to quote as a missing license grant.

Registry procedure:
- Record each reviewed source's exact revision and data scope, verdict, primary evidence URLs, short quoted clauses, decision date and status.
- A ban or exception must name the decision-maker, timestamp, exact source and revision, permitted use, evidence and rationale, and link back to this issue. Permission for one revision or code artifact does not silently extend to another dataset.
- Review backfill findings before adding them as bans or changing existing admissions. An unresolved audit row is not a retroactive admission decision. The script never applies an admission or ban diff: the user approves it. Active source bans remain binding until a recorded user lift.

Done when:
- [ ] Every current Atlas source has a primary-evidence license receipt or an explicit unresolved audit row.
- [ ] New ingestion and admission fail before other ingest stages without permission or an explicit exception.
- [ ] Reviewed blocked sources and subsequent permission changes remain recorded here with evidence.

spillover_issues.body:
`iris task exec` returns `Error: 'NoneType' object has no attribute 'decode'` when the selected task has no live container. The response hides the task state and prevents a caller from distinguishing an unavailable container from a failed command.

Reproduce:
1. Select an owned Kubernetes task whose latest attempt is pending after preemption, or whose job has completed.
2. Run `uv run iris --cluster=marin task exec --timeout 20 /OWNER/JOB/0 -- /bin/echo probe-ok`.
3. Observe the decode error instead of a missing-live-container diagnostic. The same pending-task probe failed through the direct `cw-us-east-02a` controller.

Expected: report that there is no live container, with the current task/attempt state. This report does not establish a failure to execute commands in running containers.

Observed on 2026-11-16 UTC with two owned jobs in `cw-us-east-02a`:

- `new-rl-ingest-b-cascade-combined-v1`: the job had already succeeded when the 00:09:55 probe returned the decode error.
- `new-rl-ingest-b-openresearcher-grounding-v6/inference-worker-66188b7dbe2440799d33a4705dbf9e75-0`: attempt 0 was preempted; attempt 1 was `building`, with `SchedulingGated` awaiting an H100. Both `/bin/echo` and a process-list probe returned the same error.

A control on the running owned `new-rl-ingest-b-openresearcher-kaniko-v3` job returned `probe-ok`. The local CLI revision for the completed-task and direct-controller probes was `6a5cd0bb5d1baddcf0a46c6b2ae9b58de31f54df`; the deployed controller revision was not recorded. The cause of the decode failure is unconfirmed.

comments.body:
🤖
# Research

`iris task exec` routes the current attempt to the K8s backend even when the task is pending or complete. The backend derives a pod name without checking whether that pod is running, then calls the Kubernetes exec stream; the reported `NoneType.decode` error appears to come from that call when no live container is available.

**Relevant code**
- [`attempts.py#L236-L269`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/83ab8b902e/lib/iris/src/iris/cluster/controller/attempts.py#L236-L269) — controller exec routing
- [`tasks.py#L2797-L2812`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/83ab8b902e/lib/iris/src/iris/cluster/backends/k8s/tasks.py#L2797-L2812) — pod name resolution
- [`tasks.py#L2875-L2894`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/83ab8b902e/lib/iris/src/iris/cluster/backends/k8s/tasks.py#L2875-L2894) — K8s exec

# Proposed Fix

The CLI calls the controller, which passes the current attempt to the K8s provider; the provider calls Kubernetes exec without a live-pod check. Return an exec error with the recorded task and attempt state when the task is not running, and report the pod phase or absence when the selected pod is not running. Keep the running-pod path intact.

The safe Iris suite passed on current `main` (3,045 passed).

The older Datakit evaluation reference collection has a recorded coverage gap: its CoreWeave v3 manifest lists 121 failed lm-eval-harness (LMH) task requests, including GSM8K, original MMLU, TruthfulQA and TriviaQA. Preparation deliberately continued after individual failures while requiring the nine Artificial Analysis benchmarks to succeed. These are failed task requests, some of which share a dataset or expand into multiple subjects; they are not counts of contaminated training rows. [#10541](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/10541) repairs core loading and adds required-task gates, while [#11499](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/11499) adds the separate Micro210/SWE-bench/holdout references. This task covers the remaining extraction gaps, review of the proposed replacement sources, and measurement of consequences for past data releases.

At #10541 head `a7facbd9f0cf627f359bdeaf1d0d14f1027f3358`:

- The `gsm8k` → `openai/gsm8k` loader mapping fixes both `gsm8k` and `gsm8k_cot`. Only `gsm8k` becomes required.
- Retrying required task loads and requiring all MMLU leaves addresses the v3 `mmlu` network failure. The staged v5 manifest includes all 57 original MMLU subjects.
- The five required task names are `gsm8k`, `humaneval`, `mmlu`, `mmlu_pro` and `leaderboard_mmlu_pro`. HumanEval and both MMLU-Pro variants were already represented in v3; the new gates protect future preparations.
- `leaderboard_math_hard` and `minerva_math` also load in the staged v5 corpus, but this diff adds neither their missing dependencies nor required-task gates. Treat this as observed recovery in that preparation environment, not a guaranteed dependency repair.

The actual v5 failure set is exactly the v3 set minus those five recovered requests; it has 116 entries and no new failures. The distinction matters: the diff directly addresses three v3 failed requests, while two more recover in the staged artifacts without a specific code fix.

| Failure category | Failed v3 requests | Still failed in staged v5 | Remaining examples/work |
|---|---:|---:|---|
| Unavailable task names | 54 | 54 | 40 `include_base_44_*` and 14 `mmmlu_*` requests; map to current evaluated tasks or explicitly retire them after review |
| Unsupported dataset-loading scripts | 40 | 40 | Arithmetic, CMMLU, CrowS-Pairs, ethics, LogiQA and others; review pinned direct extraction within the existing preparation path |
| Invalid unnamespaced dataset IDs | 22 | 20 | ANLI, BoolQ/COPA, TriviaQA, TruthfulQA and others; GSM8K variants are handled by #10541 |
| Missing optional grading dependencies | 4 | 2 | `ifeval` and `leaderboard_ifeval` still fail for missing `langdetect`; keep the two recovered math groups reproducible |
| Disconnected download | 1 | 0 | Original MMLU is handled by #10541's retry/required-task changes |
| Total | 121 | 116 | Counts describe requests, not independent benchmark families |

The separate `atlas-eval-coverage-v2` supplement, built before #11499 was narrowed, maps the 121 requests onto 107 replacement source families. Nonzero output and checksum validation do not establish equivalent benchmark versions, test splits, row selection, or extracted text. One concrete scope difference needs an explicit decision: the proposed `leaderboard_math_hard` replacement indexes 5,000 full MATH test records, whereas its staged v5 harness leaves contain 1,324 hard-subset records. A conservative superset may be intentional, but its removal consequences and scope must be documented. The `atlas-eval-coverage-v2` supplement also omits 1,122 LMH records because exact copies fail the unchanged matcher: 13-word n-grams, 0.5 paragraph overlap and at least two matched features (including its guarded short-text feature rules). The [feature policy](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/17d8dae0c536f8946b440dbdd626ddf58a6047f3/lib/marin/src/marin/datakit/decon.py#L479) defines the exact-copy criterion; the supplement manifest records each omitted ID.

A fresh regional replay reproduced the reported 16,887 → 421,159 exact-copy detections over the same supplement reference records; each probe tests whether an exact copy of extracted evaluation text is flagged. Of the 404,272 additional positive probes, 400,887 come from LMH replacements and 3,385 from the new benchmark/holdout references. Those are reference probes; they do not measure newly flagged training rows or model-score inflation. Historical Atlas/SFT mark and training-store lineage has not been established; the old/new flagged-row delta under unchanged document-frequency filters and matching thresholds remains unmeasured. [#6852](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/6852) separately tracks matching-policy precision/recall.

- v3 manifest: `s3://marin-us-east-02a/marin/datakit/decontam/evals/aa-index-v4.1.1-v3/lmh/_manifest.json` ([Filer](https://filer.marina.oa.dev/#s3%3A%2F%2Fmarin-us-east-02a%2Fmarin%2Fdatakit%2Fdecontam%2Fevals%2Faa-index-v4.1.1-v3%2Flmh%2F_manifest.json)).

- Reconcile all 121 original failed requests with #10541's required tasks, the 116 staged-v5 failures and current evaluation requirements. Record aliases, expanded leaf tasks, expected counts, and any explicitly retired/optional task with a reason.

spillover_issues.body: # Hypothesis / goal H0: Short RL training (<200 steps) cannot teach a task-specific skill but only re-usable skills (e.g. using agentic harness). H1: RL does teach task-specific skills. # Method Definitions: - We call transferrable (or re-usable skills) a capabilities that can be applied to different tasks and do not depend on the specific task context. Examples: tool usage, efficient context usage etc. - On the other hand, the skills that are only useful for specific tasks we will call task-specific. They help with certain tasks/contexts but cannot be applied universally and therefore are not helpful in general. To determine whether RL only teaches transferrable skills we conduct following experiments: - Exp 1: RL on the non-agentic base. Non-agentic model is not familiar with the specific harness, so RL needs to teach this capability first. If RL is capable of pushing task-specific skill further we should see continuous improvement in pass@1 (reward). However, if RL only teaches how to use the harness we would expect rising reward in the beginning and then plateau (model effectively learned how to use the harness but it doesn't improve in actual task solution and RL exhausted what it can squeeze from the policy). Note: this does not mean that it's the case (it can be something else like exploration collapse) but it's one evidence that will count towards H0. Therefore, exp 1 on it's own is not enough to disprove H1. - Exp 2: RL on agentic base (already knows how to use the harness). Evidence for H1: reward should climb - RL can teach capability beyond harness usage. If reward is flat it's another evidence towards H0. - Exp 3: RL on agentic base with a different harness. If H0 holds, the behavior should be similar to Exp 1 - reward rises up in the beginning and thne plateaus. - Exp 4: RL that rewards transferrable skills beyond harness usage. Construct tasks that require some re-usable skill in order to solve and reward the model for efficient usage of that skill. Rising reward here would also support H0 (though is not a clear evidence against H1). All together Exp. 1-4 should provide enough evidence to prove or disprove H0. We don't test RL transfer (i.e. agent performance on OOD tasks) since we only care about training dynamics and the transfer is a separate question. # Status In the process of consolidating the empirical evidence. ## Exp 1 Qwen3-8B (no agentic) on [code-contests](https://huggingface.co/datasets/DCAgent/code-contests-noblock) dataset and terminus-2 harness. We see rapid increase in training reward in just 15 steps in the beginning and then a plateau. This behavior is consistent with "the non-agentic model first learned how to use the harness and how to behave in the agentic workflows". Then RL just stops being useful. For comparison, I also did the same setup but [g1](https://huggingface.co/DCAgent/g1_diverse_tezos_100k_8b) (agentic SFT on top of Qwen3-8B). However, both improve their token efficiency (base -10% and g1 -15% in avg response length), this is supports H0 - a systematic behavioral skill that RL can teach a model. ## Exp 2 Ran [g1](https://huggingface.co/DCAgent/g1_diverse_tezos_100k_8b) (Qwen3-8B trained on teacher traces with terminus-2 harness) on R2E-Gym dataset with ctx len 81k (yarn factor=2). Harness: terminus-2 (t2) - native for g1. Longer context was used because for r2e tasks and terminus-2 more than half of rollouts are useless - they crash with CLE. Trained for 84 steps. Reward over 84 steps: 0.326->0.375, p@8: 0.516->0.609. The reward slope shrinks from +0.00086 to +0.00032/step as more steps are added (a plateau), not a slow climb that just needed room. pass@8 is visibly pinned at ~0.60 from step 10 onward. There's areal policy movement shown by KL climbing but almost no improvement in pass rate. ## Exp 3 Same configuration as Exp 2 but with terminus-structured harness and native 40k ctx len for Qwen (t-struct has better context management than t2 ). Trained for 140 steps. Reward over 140 steps: 0.24 -> 0.35 (almost the same p@1 as g1 on t2 starts from i.e. no real capability gain). p@: 0.47->0.58 (again g1 t2 starts at 0.58). ## Exp 4 [g1](https://huggingface.co/DCAgent/g1_diverse_tezos_100k_8b) on [SWE-smith-py-code-search](https://huggingface.co/datasets/OpenHands/SWE-smith-py-code-search). The task is code localization and not bug fixes. The reward function is $R=R^{F1-file}+R^{F1-module}+R^{F1-entity}$ sum of F1 scores for each granularity (file-, module-, entity-based localization). We see that for g1 the reward monotonically grows - the model learns to efferently search and at the same time becomes more efficient (avg response length drops). For each granularity level, we see that entity-level is the hardest and the steepest while file-level is almost saturated. spillover_issues.body:
Relevant work: #6521, [MATES](https://arxiv.org/abs/2406.06046), [Group-MATES](https://arxiv.org/abs/2502.14709), [RegMix](https://arxiv.org/abs/2407.01492v2), [RegMix-D](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.18663), [Meta-rater](https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.14194), [DataMan](https://arxiv.org/abs/2502.19363), [Scalable Influence and Fact Tracing](https://arxiv.org/abs/2410.17413), [DoGE](https://arxiv.org/abs/2310.15393v2)

tl;dr: We should label our data on a bunch of axes (downstream performance, LLM oracle, gradient alignment, etc) and cluster over those axes (and domain) to create buckets for the data mixing swarms

The literature on pre-training data selection has moved fairly significantly beyond FineWeb-Edu style pipelines where you use an LLM-as-judge to rate a sample set of your pretraining data and then train a small model to predict those scalar labels across your pretraining data. 

The first and most important change is treating quality as a multi-dimensional label. In DataMan 14 quality criteria and 15 domains labels are used; in Meta-rater data is labeled on professionalism, readability, reasoning, and cleanliness and proxy models are trained to learn the most useful combination of the signals for validation loss. A scale-up of this approach looks like [propella-1](https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.12414v1)--Qwen3 models which produce structured JSON over 18 properties in six categories. 

The second change is moving to approaches that don't rely on an LLM oracle like downstream performance or gradient alignment. This changes include the further insight that these labels are dynamic (treating each label as conditional on training state/progress). For instance, MATES calculates loss of a model at step t after training on candidate points. DoGE calculates a gradient alignment for full domain buckets.

New work on pretraining data selection has also emphasized the importance of diversity and group-level view of utility. Group-MATES shows that the influence scores of documents cannot be considered independently, and groups documents using their individual influence scores. [Spokes](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.15216) emphasizes the importance of diversity as a set-level attribute, meaning that buckets themselves should likely get labels as well.

The goal then is a vector of labels per training document, which then get clustered into groups, which can be selected over by our swarms.

Our particular setting and fusing the prior work into one pipeline introduces a few questions but also resolves a few difficulties:
* We are only trying to produce buckets: Meta-rater and Group-MATES think about both the labels and how to select over the labels, we only need to produce the most informative labels possible
* We will/do have training trajectories from model trained over substantially similar data to (presumably) what we will train on in the future. This potentially gives us more signal for model-based labels. However, naively using our checkpoints introduces the danger of only incorporating a memorization/exposure signal rather than a data property itself
* Should our clusters be independent of domain or include domain as another label? (my prior is domain should be included to create clusters)
* The cost and "unity" of the labeler:
   * We could do something like propella-1 where we have a fairly large model predict our entire vector at once. However, this means we introduce a large global barrier into quality labeling work: we can get labels once all have been finalized and the labeler is trained<sup>*</sup>. Additionally, we introduce ~5,000 B200-GPU hours of cost (1B labeler, FP4) to label our training set
   * Alternatively, we train models for each axis we care about at ~the size of our current quality labeler (40M). This allows work on axes to not block each other, but at 20 axes (pessimistically 12 due to small model MFUs) we end up using the same number of GPU hours, for a presumably worse result than predicting all axes at once with a larger model


\* Something like training LoRAs per axis and folding them into the model as we add new axes could work as we expand our set of labels, but also means introducing additional risk as we are stacking multiple bets at once when moving to this approach

comments.author: muchanem
comments.body: A lot of the information is probably directly linearly decodable from the embeddings and doesn't require training a separate model (e.g. for the quality labels, like 90% of the performance of our current model can be captured by a linear probe on the document embedding). But, it's important that the projection be learned--the dominant variance in the embeddings is topic/genre, and so clustering on the embeddings directly (or after a random projection) wouldn't recover things like the MATES downstream performance metric or gradient alignment. So the labels can be understood as making the axes we care about dominant under the clustering metric rather than averaged out. I do also suspect some axes may also turn out to have no signal above label noise in Harrier at all, so we would need to train a separate model.

Sounds good! Yeah, I think the baseline would be to try your workflow for quality on other axes we care about and only expand to a custom model for axes we have high confidence & evidence will lead to improvements.

The fact that the expensive compute isn't re-usable is what I don't like about the Propella approach. comments.author: ClassicLarry
comments.body:
I am not well-read in datamixing literature and what actually works- but just a general thought on optimization.

In any open-ended optimization problem, a big decision is how to coalesce the search space into a tractable number of degrees of freedom (EG should we have a learning rate per parameter, or one global LR, or a learning rate per parameter per step). 

To me, every degree of freedom is inherently a bad thing. It exponentially grows the search space, increases risk of overfitting, and makes it harder to interpret results. And it is only worth including a degree of freedom when it empirically proves its worth. I also find it easy to underestimate the future inertia that degrees of freedom introduce. (EG if we fit a unique LR to MLP up projection, suddenly moving to Latent MoE means there is a lot more work to do to retune).

On DataMan 14 quality criteria, my first thought would be "how many of these can we remove without significantly hurting performance". I think its great to test a very large number of hypothesis during exploration phase, but afterwards, every degree of freedom of the system should be sensitive to the objective function- otherwise it should be pruned. I think its easy to get into the reverse mindset, where degrees of freedom are viewed as implying sophistication of the system (but I think this is backwards).

comments.author: muchanem
comments.body: I largely agree--I think the final design will include a step of clustering over all (or all but domain) of the axes, so our search space should stay small and ideally reducing risk of overfitting. However, even in this case we've reduced interpretability a lot, since each bucket is now an "agglomeration of a bunch of factors we think might be relevant" as opposed to something clean like "high quality agent transcripts". I think selecting our axes by how much they change our clustering might be a good approach to maintaining discipline on the number of degrees of freedom we introduce!

spillover_issues.body:
**Agent-driven issue** — filed by a Claude agent, supervised by @mcwitt.

262,144 is the stated context target for the Grug hero shape (#8141) and for extending the 67B-A2B after its 10T run, but no open issue tracks what stands in the way. The epics that used to hold this picture are all closed (#2062, #6047, #1370, #4276, #6656), none of the 14 gates in #8233 mentions sequence length, and #8141 covers attention-kernel qualification only.

The longest sequence trained anywhere so far is 65,536, on TPU v4-2048: two completed cooldowns (#6811, 211B tokens, Paloma macro 2.2772; #6044, 211.3B tokens, 2.224) and a third 1T-token leg running now. On GB200, 65k has run only as short `mhep-ctxext-*` ladder jobs that reached between 100 and 500 of 800 scheduled steps before crashing (#7956). Nothing above 65,536 has trained on any platform.

Blockers, ordered by what gates what.

**Context parallelism is unqualified.** #8141 targets a `data=16, context=4` mesh on 64 GB200s, holding tokens per rank at 65,536. The blocker is the GPU image. TE 2.17.1 fails cuDNN backward graph construction with `CUDNN_STATUS_BAD_PARAM` at `fused_attn_f16_arbitrary_seqlen.cu:934`, reproducing on NVIDIA's own CP4 Ring control at B2/S65536, and the newer TE cannot source-build because `$CUDA_HOME/nvvm/bin/cicc` is absent. `lib/marin/src/marin/inference/vllm_server.py` already solves that nvvm layout problem for the vLLM/FlashInfer toolchain. No 64-GPU run has been submitted, and the branch has been idle since 2026-08-11.

**Grug cannot express a sharded sequence axis.** `_GRUG_MESH_AXIS_NAMES` in `lib/levanter/src/levanter/grug/sharding.py` is `("replica_dcn", "data", "expert", "model")`, with no context slot, and `_assert_sequence_axis_unsharded` in `lib/levanter/src/levanter/grug/attention/_fa4_cute.py` rejects sharded q/k/v. Haliax has `ResourceAxis.CONTEXT` with a parity test (#2187, #2188), but that path shards Q and replicates KV on splash attention only, so it does not relieve per-device KV at 262k.

**MoE drop rate at few documents per shard is unmeasured.** Drop rate is governed by cell size and documents per shard, because tokens within a document route coherently and the effective sample size is the document count rather than the token count (#8046). The hero runs 16 documents per shard. At 262k with the token budget held fixed the batch is 16 sequences per rack, so EP64 would see 0.25. #6170 measured overflow fraction roughly doubling per 4x sequence length at EP2, with tokens per step held constant. #8062 specified the arm that would settle this at hero scale, EP64 at 65k seqlen and batch 64, and those jobs are the ones that crashed in #7956 without reporting a drop rate or loss.

**Nothing evaluates past 32k.** The `long_context_32k` bundle caps there, and PG19 is the only slice where sequence length still matters at that point. RULER has not landed in a suite (#7638), and `experiments/evals/long_context_ppl.py` was deleted in #6633. Every 65k result to date is Paloma macro loss against a target preregistered at seqlen 8192, which shows the transition is stable without showing that the model uses the added context.

**Memory headroom is about 1 GiB.** The hero peaks at 137.21 GiB against a 138.22 GiB allocator cap and runs only because that keeps `HloRematerialization` off (#8054). All 48 layers share one `jax.scan` and therefore one remat policy, so global and local layers cannot carry different policies.

Two costing notes for anyone picking this up. #8141 is scoped against the FSDP hero's 512/every-6 attention, while the EP hero moved to 2048/every-4 (#8132, #8227), giving 12 global layers instead of 8. Any 64-device one-shot symmetric collective needs the patched PJRT wheel from #8077, since stock XLA caps `kMaxPeers` at 32.

Done when:

- [ ] #8141 passes its four-GPU CP4 forward/backward gate and reports compile time, steady-state time, peak HBM, and gradient parity at B16/S262144.
- [ ] The #8062 context-extension arm reruns and posts a drop rate and loss at 65k with fewer sequences per batch.
- [ ] A long-context capability eval (RULER or needle-style retrieval) runs on an existing 65k checkpoint.
- [ ] Grug has a context mesh axis with parameters and optimizer state sharded over composite `(data, context)`.
- [ ] EP is shown to compose with CP at long context, or the 262k path records a decision to run FSDP-only. #6656 found degenerate expert routing with EP>1 and CP>1 at 131k in the RL stack.

<!-- experiment-tldr:start -->
## Summary

This issue tracks grug MoE quantile-balancing ablations that compare the existing chunk-quantile averaging estimator against per-sequence, fixed logit histogram, K3 sigmoid histogram, dynamic histogram, and after-sigmoid variants. The planned d768/d1024/d1280 sweep did not fully run as originally scoped: the estimator comparison that executed on August 7-8, 2026 was d768 only, while separate QB-bias runs covered d768/d1024/d1280. The useful current state is the run map in the August 17 update, including two crashed histogram variants; the issue still needs a final loss/load-balance synthesis before changing the default estimator.

### Helpful links
- [Run map comment](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/8033#issuecomment-5320860256)
- [CHUNK_QUANTILE baseline: qb-abl-normal](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/runs/qb-abl-normal)
- [PER_SEQUENCE: qb-abl-perseq](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/runs/qb-abl-perseq)
- [LOGIT_HIST: qb-abl-logithist](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/runs/qb-abl-logithist)
- [K3_HIST: qb-abl-k3hist](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/runs/qb-abl-k3hist)
<!-- experiment-tldr:end -->

## Description

grug MoE balances expert load with **QB**: each step it overwrites the per-expert router bias from a target quantile of each expert's routing scores over the batch (top-4 of 128 experts). Two families estimate that quantile:

- **Chunk-quantile / averaging** — exact `(1−k/n)` quantile per chunk, then average. Chunk = per-GPU shard (current `local` default, topology-dependent) or per-sequence (topology-independent). "Histogram vs Avg" refers to this averaging family.
- **Histogram** — accumulate a per-expert histogram, read one quantile. `logit_hist` (fixed logit range) or `k3_hist` (Kimi-K3, sigmoid-score space, adaptive `[bmin−1, bmax+1]` range).

Two known concerns motivate the sweep:
- **Dropping / coverage.** A fixed-range logit histogram silently **drops** out-of-range values (`jnp.histogram` excludes them rather than clamping), truncating the upper tail and biasing the `~0.969` target quantile. Score-space (K3) is bounded to `[0,1]` so it covers by construction; logit-space is unbounded and does not.
- **Histogram vs averaging.** A prior simple histogram was found worse than chunk-quantile (binning + range-calibration error beating the histogram's theoretical unbiasedness); we want to quantify this cleanly and see whether the K3 score-space histogram closes the gap.

## Hypothesis / Goal

Identify the best QB estimator for grug MoE by loss **and** load-balance quality, and settle:
1. **Histogram vs averaging** — reproduce and quantify the gap on matched configs.
2. **Dropping / coverage** — measure token-drop rate and expert-load imbalance per estimator, plus histogram out-of-range coverage (logit min/max, fraction outside range).
3. **Topology-independence** — per-sequence chunk-quantile vs per-device `local`.

Estimators under test (`experiments/grug/moe_hero_fsdp/model.py`, `qb_estimator`):
- `local` — per-device chunk-quantile (current default)
- per-sequence chunk-quantile (new, topology-independent)
- `logit_hist` — fixed-range logit histogram (+ coverage instrumentation / clamp variant)
- `k3_hist` — adaptive sigmoid-score histogram

## Setup (planned)

- **Ablation sizes:** d768, d1024, d1280 (downsized grug MoE hero shape; architecture/data/eval/optimizer/steps held fixed, vary only `qb_estimator`).
- **Metrics:** paloma macro loss, uncheatable bpb, per-expert load balance (max/mean load, drop rate), and for histograms the out-of-range coverage fraction.

## Status

Runs were launched for the d768 estimator comparison and the three-size QB-bias checks. A final metric synthesis is still needed before making a recommendation.

## Links

* Logbook:
* W&B Report:
* Important updates: https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/8033#issuecomment-5320860256

## Decision Log

## Conclusion

Part of #6711

A high-level, deliberately loosely-scoped **wish-list of new evals for Marin**. Some of these are straightforward to build; others are hard design problems that may require several evals to satisfy. **This list is non-comprehensive and will grow over time** — it is a living backlog, not a fixed spec.

## How to work on something from this list

To pick up an item:

1. **Open a focused sub-issue** that explicitly references this epic and names the item it addresses (e.g. *"Picks up item 3 (arbitrary tool use) of #<this epic>"*). Scope the actual eval design there.
2. **Comment on this epic** linking the sub-issue, so the item is marked as **now independently tracked**. Check its box below.

The checkboxes track which items have a home yet — an unchecked box means "open for someone to pick up."

## The wish-list

- [ ] **1 — Better IFBench + IFEval.** By "better" we mean primarily *more nuanced and capturing more of human "intuition"* about when autonomy is to be preferred — e.g. **when is it acceptable for an agent to override a user's stated aims?** This can arise because: users ask for contradictory (or seemingly-contradictory-out-of-context) things that the agent may misread as being in direct conflict; the user makes a mistake writing the request; the request is adversarial w.r.t. the model's constitution; or the agent acquires new information the user did not have when making the request which, had the user had it, would likely have changed the initial request.

- [ ] **2 — Agentless "baby-TB" (harness-less, few-turn terminal tasks).** The agent solves terminal tasks in a terminus-2-esque non-harness: all tool calls are simple JSON, the only tool is `bash`. Tasks should be solvable in just a few steps.

- [ ] **3 — Arbitrary tool use.** Perhaps with dynamically sourced tools from real APIs, MCP endpoints, and harnesses: **can the model use *any* unseen tool with sufficient documentation correctly?** The key is to hit tools that are very unlikely to have appeared in the pretraining corpus.

- [ ] **4 — Structured generation.** How reliably can the model produce **large amounts of compliant data** in common formats (YAML, JSON, XML, XLSX, CSV, TSV)?

- [ ] **5 — Subagent lifecycle management and redirection.** How effectively can the model respond to summaries produced by subagents, catch errors made by (potentially weaker) subagent models, and devise appropriate remedies, etc.?

- [ ] **6 — Basic numeracy failure modes.** The classic LLM traps: the `9.9 < 9.11` meme, the "how many r's in strawberry" meme, correct simple arithmetic with large numbers — **or** deciding to fall back on tools when appropriate.

- [ ] **7 — Sense of time.** The agent should be habituated to the fact that it is an agent and **does not know what time or day it is right now**, nor how long has elapsed since it was last prompted, and should behave appropriately.

- [ ] **8 — Check facts before responding / grounding.** Confirm that the agent always *checks the facts before responding when it is possible*, and *does not attempt to when it is not possible*. More generally: how well does the agent **ground its answers in real, available context** when responding?

- [ ] **9 — "Who am I".** The agent should robustly know **who and what it is**, even when it is in a chat harness or is asked to roleplay a persona.

- [ ] **10 — Scalable-difficulty proxy for GDPval-AA v2.**

- [ ] **11 — Scalable-difficulty proxy for 𝜏³-Banking.**

- [ ] **12 — Scalable-difficulty proxy for SciCode.**

- [ ] **13 — Scalable-difficulty proxy for AA-Omniscience.**

- [ ] **14 — Self-compaction efficiency and precision.** When the model compacts/summarizes its own context: **does its recall agree with human recall?** And **how much of the context window is consumed by the model's self-summary?** (i.e. both fidelity and cost of self-compaction.)

- [ ] **15 — Knowing how long to think.** Can the model correctly calibrate **how many tokens to spend thinking**, based on a correct assessment of (A) how hard the problem is and (B) whether the model has any realistic chance of getting it right with what it has available?

- [ ] **16 — Robustness to prompt noise and irrelevant context.** Response quality should be insensitive to **user-prompting imprecision** (whitespace, linebreaks, typos, and other common noise), and insensitive to **irrelevant prior context** — if the chat history is full of garbage or unrelated content, the model should still respond intelligently to the *latest* request.

---

*Items 10–13 are "suitable proxy with scalable difficulty" targets for the named external benchmarks. New items will be appended as the wish-list grows; renumbering is avoided so existing sub-issue references stay stable.*

spillover_issues.author: ravwojdyla-agent
spillover_issues.body:
## Description

Build **smallquery**: self-serve, BigQuery-like SQL analytics over our Parquet datasets on object storage (regional GCS and CoreWeave), running on Iris and using spare capacity on preemptible VMs. A user submits a SQL query through an API or dashboard and gets the result back in object storage to stream or download.

Design and implementation notes (the *how*) live in `.agents/projects/smallquery/` and `lib/smallquery/`. This issue tracks the **system requirements**, not the design.

## System requirements

- **Distributed execution with shuffle** — must run joins and high-cardinality `GROUP BY` across many workers, not single-node only. (Hard requirement.)
- **Preemption-tolerant** — workers run on preemptible VMs that can vanish at any moment; a query must still complete with correct results, without restarting from scratch.
- **Scales beyond one node** — handles queries whose working set exceeds a single VM's memory.
- **Opportunistic / good neighbour** — uses spare CPU/RAM and yields to higher-priority work; never starves co-located jobs.
- **Data-local, egress-aware** — computes in the same region/cloud as the data; rejects (or explicitly gates) queries that would cause cross-region egress.
- **Durable results** — materializes the full result to object storage (stream/download) plus a quick, size-capped inline preview.
- **Self-serve access** — a query API and a dashboard reachable on the Iris cluster.
- **Governed access** — datasets referenced by name through a catalog with per-dataset authorization; no raw object-store paths in user SQL (potentially integrated with the artifact registry).
- **Correct** — results match a single-node reference engine over the same data.

## Dependencies

- A per-node worker-fleet capability on Iris (#6763).

## Definition of Done (capabilities)

- [ ] A join and a high-cardinality `GROUP BY` run **distributed** and return correct results.
- [ ] Killing workers mid-query does not fail or corrupt the query — it still returns the correct result.
- [ ] Runs on spare/preemptible capacity and yields to higher-priority jobs.
- [ ] Results land in object storage and are reachable via the API + dashboard on both GCS and CoreWeave.
- [ ] Cross-region queries are rejected or explicitly gated per the egress policy.
- [ ] Results validated equal to a single-node reference.
- [ ] Design doc reviewed/merged.

comments.body:
The option in one picture: a persistent non-preemptible coordinator (API + dashboard) + a fleet of warm preemptible workers; queries become a DAG of shards that exchange chunks through object storage (never local disk); results to a TTL'd location + capped preview.

Key choices — each had a real alternative:
- Distributed + object-store shuffle ↔ single-node big-RAM (evaluated, rejected — distributed was a hard requirement; cf. https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/6760)
- Object-store shuffle ↔ local-disk shuffle on an SSD scratch group (would unlock off-the-shelf Spark/Trino).
- New IrisDaemon per-node primitive ↔ standing pool / per-query jobs.
- Per-attempt _SUCCESS manifest committer ↔ atomic-rename / conditional-create.
- Thin coordinator + embedded SQLite snapshotted to GCS ↔ reconcile-by-listing / Postgres.
- Kernel: DataFusion vs DuckDB left as a measured bake-off.
- Python coordinator (logical-plan cutting) + Rust workers ↔ Rust coordinator shipping physical plans.
- Skew: fail cheaply ↔ salting/spill.

Prior art: borrowed finelog (deployment/dashboard/SQLite-checkpoint) and zephyr (object-store scatter, retry tiers); the Spice AI Ballista fork is the only OSS object-store shuffle but recomputes durable data on writer loss (our committer avoids that); ClickHouse/smallpond/Polars rejected for our constraints.

One practically and lazy option would be to borrow useful parts/components of DataFusion/Ballista and sprinkle it with parts that require custom handling.

comments.author: alxmrs
comments.body:
Here are my thoughts and impressions about which technology choices to make for the smallquery project: 

## DuckDB vs Polars vs DataFusion

These are all very similar but I think there are some important  differences that will lead us to decide that DataFusion is the right RDBMS engine to build atop of. 

Here is DataFusion's explanation of the differences between each project: https://datafusion.apache.org/user-guide/faq.html#how-does-datafusion-compare-with-xyz

- DuckDB vs DataFusion: Both are very similar in goal (in process/embeddable OLAP query engine). DuckDB is built around its own internal format whereas DataFusion is designed to be agnostic of the core DB format. 
- DuckDB vs DataFusion: Both are modular and extensible, but DataFusion is the natural ancestor to Apache Arrow; see this post on [Composable Data Systems](https://wesmckinney.com/blog/looking-back-15-years/)
- DuckDB vs (DataFusion & Polars): C++ (sometimes, with Rust Extensions) vs a pure-rust ecosystem -- my preference is to go with Rust.
- Polars vs the rest: Polars is built on arrow, but is not designed as a "deconstructed database" like DuckDB and DataFusion, so it will be harder to integrate with. 

## Distribution 

Assuming DataFusion is the bet we go with, the next open question is Comet vs Ballista vs DataFusion Distributed: 

- Comet is DataFusion/Arrow within Spark, so I see this as really saying we should go with (better) Spark. While this is faster than Spark, it is still the slowest option in the distributed DataFusion ecosystem. This is lowest on my list, primarily because it adds a lot of system complexity (I count ~4-5 layers of abstraction between Zephyr, Spark, Comet, DataFusion, and Iris). The benefit, however, is that Comet happened to be a more popular choice than Ballista, even though I think Ballista is a better system. I think this might have to do with the amount of buy-in/popularity of Apache Spark.
- Ballista is the most mature way of distributing DataFusion. However, the DataFusion-Python to Ballista Python integration is somewhat far behind the primary version of DataFusion, making it suspect for us to want to depend on. (Warning: I could be wrong about this impression -- this is from recently trying to build on top of Ballista with Python a few months ago).
- DataFusion-Distributed is the new distributed system for DataFusion, and its core promise is to be a natural extension of the DataFusion data model (logical and physical plans). https://datafusion-contrib.github.io/datafusion-distributed/. I like this choice for Iris because it delegates full control over how plans are distributed over workers, so I think it would give us more power to handle retries and preemption in an iris layer rather than the DB layer. It also should delegate to Iris actors with a more lightweight interface than Ballista. I also like that it looks like this system will be integrated into DataFusion-Python soon: https://github.com/apache/datafusion-python/issues/1612. That said, the concerns that Will pointed out from the "when not to use this section" may be dealbreakers, and the right bet is to integrate Ballista into Iris workers. 

I also just posted in the DataFusion Discord to ask what the maintainers recommend. It might be that the best way to find out would be to build a small prototype with DataFusion.

## Responses to the above discussion

>  still doesn't mean you couldn't use the same distributed sql engine with scheduling similar to Zephyr's today for the larger data processing jobs.
> Why only share the shuffle? Presumably smallquery has would also need to do distributed maps for certain queries?
> there's no reason it couldn't also handle the things written in Python / Zephyr today.

I am 100% on this team; I think a SQL engine is the core thing you need for doing ELT/ETL, even for [non-tabular data](https://github.com/jayendra13/zarr-datafusion).

> How much of this could we reuse from Datafusion/Ballista? It looks like the main gap there would be the shuffles do temp writes to local disk. We could bring some of those ideas in though.

I agree, I think reusing DB technology is better than reinventing it, especially since distributed shuffles for reductions are non-trivial. I think DataFusion-Distributed would fit in the cleanest with Iris, if we can handle retry logic and persistence (maybe that makes Ballista the winner -- my original intention with https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/5861 was to have the DataFusion Context be swappable with a Ballista Context running on other workers in Iris). 

> ~100 sources, ~100k parquet files, ~35TB. In most cases we can assume parquet, but other formats would be nice to have.

35 TB is small. If we're looking for Marin Infra to support workloads in scientific applications like Coral, then we'd want to make sure this system scales to the 1s to 10s of petabytes IMO. We don't need to do this now, but it would be nice to know that such a thing is possible. (I still dream of loading all 12 PiBs of [ARCO-ERA5](https://github.com/google-research/arco-era5) into Marin). [Samudra](https://github.com/m2lines/Samudra), my primary project, is still looking for a core data engineering system replacement to Dask, and a 3 PiB dataset is on our roadmap to process.

> at some point I was curious if I could replace that with Arrow/Parquet, do you happen to have experience with that use-case? Scale ~20T. Actually, https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/4445 would be a good place to have this chat to keep this issue focused.

I'm part of the cult of [zarr.dev](https://zarr.dev), so I think Tensorstore on Zarr or maybe IceChunk is a better fit than parquet for Array shaped data. I think there could be a good opportunity to make a patch or extension to Orbax.

> I think it would probably look more like building sql support into Zephyr
> I'll work on a more coherent / detailed design proposal.

That's the dream. LMK if I can chat with you or collaborate on the design. I've done some work in this space.
